name: Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis Type 3 (CLN3 Disease, Juvenile NCL / Batten Disease)

clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic variants in CLN3 encoding battenin, a lysosomal/endosomal membrane protein; the classic juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, often termed Batten disease.

The presenting feature is typically rapidly progressive visual loss in a previously well school-age child, due to retinal degeneration, often initially misattributed to a primary ophthalmological problem.
Cognitive and behavioural decline, then seizures, then extrapyramidal and motor deterioration follow the visual failure over subsequent years.
Psychiatric and behavioural disturbance (anxiety, psychosis-like features, aggression) is prominent and may dominate the middle phase of the disease.
A common recurrent intragenic deletion in CLN3 accounts for a large proportion of cases and facilitates targeted molecular diagnosis.
Vacuolated lymphocytes on a peripheral blood film are a useful clue relatively specific to CLN3 among the NCLs.
Electron microscopy characteristically shows fingerprint profiles, contrasting with the granular osmiophilic deposits of CLN1 and curvilinear bodies of CLN2.
Because the enzyme-based assays used for CLN1 and CLN2 are normal in CLN3, diagnosis relies on CLN3 molecular testing supported by ophthalmology, blood film and ultrastructure.
reference.pathophysiology: CLN3 disease is caused by loss of function of battenin, the CLN3-encoded multipass transmembrane protein that resides principally in lysosomal and late-endosomal membranes. Although its precise molecular role is incompletely defined, battenin participates in lysosomal membrane trafficking, endosomal-lysosomal fusion, autophagy, lysosomal pH and ion homeostasis, and membrane lipid handling. Its deficiency leads to lysosomal dysfunction and accumulation of autofluorescent ceroid-lipofuscin storage material, rich in subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase, forming characteristic fingerprint inclusion profiles within neurons and other cells. The commonest disease allele is a recurrent intragenic deletion removing part of the gene. Disturbed autophagy, oxidative and endoplasmic-reticulum stress, calcium dysregulation, neuroinflammation with glial activation and immune dysregulation contribute to progressive neuronal loss. Retinal photoreceptors and ganglion cells are affected early, producing the characteristic initial visual failure, followed by cortical, cerebellar and basal-ganglia degeneration underlying the cognitive, behavioural, epileptic and motor features. The disease is unlike CLN1 and CLN2 in that it does not arise from a deficient soluble lysosomal enzyme, so conventional enzyme assays are unrevealing.
additionalDifferentials: Other neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, particularly juvenile-onset CLN1, CLN2 and CLN9-associated presentations
Primary retinal dystrophies such as retinitis pigmentosa or cone-rod dystrophy without neurodegeneration
Progressive myoclonic epilepsies including Lafora and Unverricht-Lundborg disease
Childhood-onset psychiatric illness when behavioural change dominates early
Wilson disease and other treatable causes of combined neuropsychiatric and movement decline
Mitochondrial disorders with retinopathy and neurodegeneration
Juvenile-onset lysosomal storage disorders and leukodystrophies
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of the CLN3 gene, including specific assessment for the common recurrent intragenic deletion
Peripheral blood film for vacuolated lymphocytes
Electron microscopy of skin, conjunctiva or lymphocytes for fingerprint profiles
Detailed ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography and optical coherence tomography documenting retinal degeneration and optic atrophy
MRI brain showing progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with thalamic and white-matter signal change
Electroencephalography for epileptiform activity as seizures emerge
Neuropsychological and behavioural assessment to characterise cognitive and psychiatric decline
redFlags: Rapidly progressive visual loss in a previously healthy school-age child
Emergence of cognitive decline and school failure following visual deterioration
New behavioural or psychiatric disturbance with hallucinations or aggression in a child
Onset of seizures added to visual and cognitive decline
Development of parkinsonism, dystonia or other movement disorder in the later course
reference.prognosis: CLN3 disease follows a protracted but relentless course over one to two decades, with blindness, dementia, epilepsy and motor decline leading to death in early adulthood; no disease-modifying therapy is established and care is supportive.
pitfalls: Attributing the early visual loss to an isolated primary retinal dystrophy and missing the underlying neurodegenerative disorder.
Managing the middle-phase behavioural and psychiatric features as a primary psychiatric illness without recognising the storage disease.
Excluding NCL because CLN1 and CLN2 enzyme assays are normal, when CLN3 requires molecular rather than enzymatic diagnosis.
Overlooking simple, informative bedside clues such as vacuolated lymphocytes on the blood film.
Confusing the fingerprint ultrastructure and clinical pattern of CLN3 with the distinct profiles and courses of CLN1 and CLN2.
references: Standard inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis consensus classification and diagnostic guidance
management: No disease-modifying therapy is established, so management is supportive and multidisciplinary
Control seizures with antiepileptic drugs such as valproate, levetiracetam and lamotrigine
Manage the prominent psychiatric and behavioural disturbance (anxiety, psychosis-like features and aggression) with psychological support and judicious psychotropic agents
Provide ophthalmology assessment and low-vision and blind-support services for the early progressive visual loss
Treat emerging parkinsonism and extrapyramidal features and give physiotherapy for motor decline
Support nutrition and swallowing with gastrostomy feeding as the disease advances
Coordinate palliative care, education and social support across the protracted course
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder, using targeted testing for the common recurrent intragenic deletion
